steps.text: **Forcing moves** leave the opponent very few choices. There are three kinds. A **check** attacks the king. A **capture** takes a piece. A **threat** is a quiet move that will win something, or mate, if ignored. The habit this lesson builds: list these first, look at every reply, then decide. It is where to look first, not proof that one of them works.

steps.caption: Black to move. The knight can check from e2. Step through the idea.

line.say: The knight checks the king, and nothing of White's can capture it.
White's king steps to h2.
The rook checks along the fourth rank. The king has no safe square: checkmate.

claims.statement: Ne2+ forces checkmate in two.
No white piece attacks the knight on e2.

steps.caption: White to move. White has three checks with the queen: to g6, h7 or g3. Only one of them is good.

claims.statement: The check on g3 forces mate in two.
The check on h7 loses the queen.
The check on g6 loses the queen.

line.say: Check along the g-file. No black piece can take the queen on g3.
Black's king steps to h7.
The queen lands on g7, guarded by the bishop on h6. The king cannot take it: checkmate.

claims.statement: No black piece attacks the queen on g3.
Qg3+ forces checkmate in two.

line.say: The bishop takes the bishop.
The knight retakes.
The queen, which waited behind the bishop, takes the knight. White has won a piece.

claims.statement: One white piece attacks g4 directly.
One black piece defends g4.
Bxg4 wins a piece along the engine line.

The queen moves away; the rook is still attacked.
The pawn takes the rook.
Black takes the pawn back. White has won a rook for a pawn.

claims.statement: After the push, the pawn attacks d7.
After the push, the pawn attacks b7.
The push wins material along the engine line.

steps.text: Why list them first? Because they **shrink the tree**. In 7,465 positions with the side to move in check (1,500 Lichess games, January 2013), the mean was 3.3 legal replies, and 86% had five or fewer [V]. In 88,464 positions with no check, the mean was 31.5 [V]. A capture usually invites one recapture [I]. [H] Naming the three kinds may also make an opponent's check or capture harder to miss.

steps.caption: White's queen has just checked from b3. Count Black's legal replies. A check can leave very few.

claims.statement: Black is in check.
Black has exactly one legal move.

line.say: Only Be6 blocks the check, and the king has no square. One legal reply.

steps.caption: Another position after a check. Now Black has four replies, of three kinds: take the checker, block, or move the king. Which is which?

claims.statement: Black is in check.
Black has exactly four legal moves.

steps.caption: The three kinds of answer. The queen can take the checker. The queen or the f-pawn can block on f5. The king can step to b8.

claims.statement: Black's four legal replies are the three kinds.

steps.text: Three kinds of answer to a check: **take** the checker, **block** between the checker and the king, or **move** the king. A knight check cannot be blocked. Sorting the replies this way makes a check easy to read to the end.

Counts from Lichess games (January 2013), recalled from an earlier run that cannot be reproduced now [R]: the best move was quiet about 70% of the time, a capture about 20 to 25%, and a check 5 to 10%, depending on how a capture with a check is counted. A reviewer's recount of 18,420 Lichess puzzles [S] found 62% begin with a check. [I] Forcing moves are where tactics hide, not where most moves are.

claims.statement: No line wins more than a pawn for White.
The engine rates the position as roughly level.

steps.text: No check exists here, and no capture wins anything. Saying so is a result, not a failure: you looked, and you can move on to quiet moves.

steps.chapter: When it works and when it fails
steps.caption: Black to move. A check is available: the knight can go to f3. Is it good?

line.say: The knight gives check.
The rook on e3 simply takes it. Black has lost a knight for nothing.

claims.statement: One white piece attacks f3.
The check is far worse than the best move.

steps.caption: The same position. This time Black plays the quiet move. Compare.

line.say: The bishop attacks the rook on e3, and the white king stands on the same diagonal behind it. The rook is pinned to the king: it cannot leave the diagonal.
White defends the rook with the king.
The bishop takes the rook with check.
The king takes the bishop. Black has won a rook for a bishop.

claims.statement: After Bc5 the bishop attacks the rook on e3.
Bc5 is the engine's best move.
Bc5 wins material along the engine line.
After Bc5 the rook on e3 has no legal move.

steps.caption: Black to move. Here the checker can be taken, and the check still wins. What is different?

line.say: The knight checks, and it also steps out of the way of the queen and bishop aimed at h2.
White takes the knight.
The queen takes on h2, backed by the bishop behind it. The king cannot recapture: checkmate.

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack f3, so the knight can be taken.
Nf3+ forces checkmate in two.

steps.text: A check can be taken and still win. It works when the taking piece is needed elsewhere, when taking opens a line to the king, or when the capture leaves a mate. [I] Ask of every reply: what does it do to my follow-up? Look back at the knight check: it also cleared the diagonal.

steps.caption: Black to move. A check that is also a capture: the queen can take on h2. Tempting?

line.say: The queen takes a pawn with check.
The knight takes the queen. Black has given a queen for a pawn.

claims.statement: Two white pieces guard h2.
The capture with check loses badly.

steps.caption: Black to move. White threatens mate on g7. Black's bishop can capture a knight. Does the capture help?

line.say: Black wins a knight. A capture, and it looks good.
But White's queen, backed by the bishop on c3, mates first.

claims.statement: If Black passed, Qxg7 would be checkmate.
Taking the knight loses at once.
The queen trade is Black's best move.

steps.caption: What a safe answer looks like. Trade off the attacker first, then take the knight. Engine line, depth 16: about level.

line.say: The queen trade removes White's attacker.
White retakes.
Now the bishop takes the knight, and the threat on g7 is gone.

claims.statement: The queen trade is Black's best move.
The engine rates the position as roughly level.

steps.text: Three ways a forcing move fails. The checking piece is **taken** and nothing is gained. The capture **costs more** than it wins. Your threat is **slower** than theirs. Before you play one, ask: what are all of the opponent's replies, including their own checks, captures and threats? Dan Heisman's term for playing without checking the opponent's forcing replies is "Hope Chess" [S].

steps.title: Same check, one change
steps.prompt: The first position is a forced win by a check. In the second, the rook has moved. In the third, a pawn far away has moved. Predict, then check.

steps.text: Forcing wins are built, not stumbled on. Three common ways [I]: **clear a line** (move a piece off a diagonal with a check, so a piece behind it attacks); **remove a guard** (capture or deflect the piece that defends the key square); **win a tempo** (make a threat the opponent must meet, then use the move you gained). Each earlier example used one of these.

steps.caption: Clear a line. Black's queen and bishop aim at h2, but their own knight stands on the diagonal. Moving it with check lets them through.

claims.statement: Nf3+ forces checkmate in two.

steps.text: Prevention is the same habit seen from the other side. Before you move, run the **opponent's** list: their checks, captures and threats. Two cures follow. Make **luft** (German for air): a pawn move that gives your king a square, so a back-rank check is no longer mate. And never grab something while a bigger threat of theirs stands. [H] "What does my move allow?" may be easier for beginners than "is it safe?", because it names three things to look for.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's king is boxed in by its own pawns. A queen sacrifice uses that: it pulls the rook away from b8.

line.say: The queen offers itself with check on the back rank.
Black takes the queen with the rook.
The white rook takes back. The king has no square: checkmate.

claims.statement: Qf8+ forces checkmate in two.

steps.caption: The same position with one change: Black's h-pawn stands on h6, so the king has the square h7. Does the sacrifice still work?

line.say: The same check.
Black takes the queen.
White takes back with check.
The king steps to h7. White has given a queen for a rook, and the king is not mated.

claims.statement: With the flight square, the sacrifice loses material along the engine line.

steps.caption: White to move. Before choosing, run Black's list. What is Black's best forcing idea?

claims.statement: If White passed, Qxg2 would be checkmate.

steps.caption: White grabs a pawn without asking.

line.say: White takes a pawn.
Black's threat was faster: the queen and the bishop both aim at g2.

claims.statement: Two black pieces attack g2.
The capture loses at once.

steps.caption: The better answer is a threat of White's own. One engine line, depth 14.

line.say: The pawn attacks both the bishop on e4 and the queen on g4. It also blocks the bishop's diagonal to g2, so the queen taking on g2 is no longer protected, and no longer mate.
Black takes the pawn.
The rook takes the bishop.
The queen takes the rook.
The pawn takes the queen. White comes out well ahead.

claims.statement: f3 is the engine's best move.
f3 wins material along the engine line.

steps.text: A **near miss** changes one detail, and the result may flip. Study the original, then ask what the detail did. Details that matter: who can take the checking piece, how many defenders a piece has, whether the king has a flight square. Details that do not: a pawn far from the action. Predict each, then check.

steps.text: Kotov's method, as summarised on Wikipedia [S], is to list candidate moves and analyse them in an organised tree. A reviewer of Aagaard's *Excelling at Chess Calculation* says he stresses that big errors often start when a key candidate is never listed [S, reviewer]. [R] Kotov also urged looking at each line once. [I] Checks, captures and threats are the cheapest candidates to list. Now the labels come off. Some positions have a forcing win; some do not, and then saying so is the right answer.

**A very old game**, traditionally credited to Légal and recalled here from memory [R]; the exact record is traditional. The last three White moves are all forcing. First the opening moves, then the moment to list White's forcing moves.

steps.caption: The opening moves. Black's bishop on g4 pins the knight on f3 to the queen on d1.

line.say: White takes the centre.
Black does the same.
The knight attacks e5.
Black defends the pawn.
The bishop aims at f7.
The bishop pins the knight to the queen.
White develops.
Black makes room for the bishop. This move allows a trap, shown next.

claims.statement: The bishop on g4 attacks the knight on f3, with the queen behind it.

steps.caption: White to move. White has two checks (Bxf7+ and Bb5+) and two captures (Nxe5 and Bxf7+). Which works?

claims.statement: Nxe5 is the engine's best move.
Bxf7+ is clearly worse than Nxe5.
Bb5+ is clearly worse than Nxe5.
White is clearly better.

steps.caption: Black took the queen, which was the mistake: taking the knight was better. White to move. Now the forcing moves finish the game.

line.say: The bishop takes a pawn with check. The king has only one square, e7.
The king steps to e7.
The knight checks from d5 and covers f6, while the knight on e5 and the bishop on f7 cover the other squares: checkmate.

Did you name **one mistake** (a check that can be taken, a capture that costs more, a threat that is slower)? This is for you to compare with the checklist.

**What to remember.**
- Forcing moves: checks, captures, threats.
- List them first. Then look at every reply.
- A check has few answers: take it, block it, or move the king.
- Forcing is not the same as good.
- Run the opponent's list before you move.
- Nothing forcing works? Say so, and move on.
